newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Commodities markets retain bearish feel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Commodities markets retain bearish feel.

text.p: Coffee prices slipped lower on Wednesday - a day when experts from the producing countries gathered in London to address this year's dramatic price hike.
But news of a threatened strike by Columbian dock workers gave support to the New York market.

London's benchmark robusta futures for May ignored that news and stuck to the bearish tone of recent days, closing down $41 at $1,657 per tonne. Dealers said speculative profit-taking knocked prices back after African and Asian origin selling dominated thin trading volume earlier on.
"Producers thought it would be timely to sell at these prices," said a trader. "Speculators who had been chasing the market up also decided to take profits."
Robusta turned around last week after a 50 percent rally lifted prices to $1,780 since the start of 1997. May futures briefly tumbled to $1,610 on Tuesday.
The rally, spurred by supply fears in arabica beans, was termed "excessive" by Columbia during Wednesday's Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) meeting.

Although traders said they expected no major decision to emerge, the talks by producers including Brazil, El Salvador, Indonesia, Ivory Coast and Uganda could draw up steps to tackle the price surge, which would be reported to the full ACPC council in May.

Producers fear the rising prices could threaten consumption in the long-term. Arabica has almost doubled since early December, recently hitting $2.00 a pound for the first time since a severe Brazilian frost in 1994 which affected coffee consumption as people switched to cheaper beverages.
Cocoa prices, meanwhile, took a step back from Tuesday's gains, to close down 18 at 1,015 stg.
Base metals on the London Metal Exchange (LME) showed a touch more sparkle after Tuesday's weak closes, a late spurt in copper boosting other industrials such as zinc and nickel.
LME three-month copper bounced off $2,300 to close at $2,325 a tonne, down $8, while aluminium ended a little firmer at $1,647 a tonne compared to $1,640.
Traders said fund liquidation was a key factor.
"It's still a bearish close and suggests that we'll come down to fill a gap that extends to $2,295," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis.
Data on warehouse stock levels, which failed to add any momentum to Tuesday's sagging market, is to be released on a daily basis from April 7, the LME said on Wednesday.
LME stock changes are at present reported twice a week, and the move marks an attempt to increase transparency of stock movements in the wake of 1996's multi-billion dollar Sumitomo Corp scandal.
LME traders said they were less than enthusiastic about the reforms.
"It's been done to appease the regulators," said one. "Twice weekly you get a bit of excitement. Reported daily, it loses the impact and that is not good for the market-place."
Precious metals also closed up after speculative selling caused setbacks on Tuesday.

Gold rose nearly $3 to $349.00 by the London close, and climbed still higher towards $353.00 later on, after trading in a tight range most of the day. Platinum and palladium also recovered from Tuesday's dives lower.
The crude oil market held on to early gains, held up by a smaller than expected rise in U.S. stocks.
Front month May Brent was up at $20.41 a barrel by 1752 GMT after touching an intraday high of $20.47.
"We are just holding onto yesterday's gains and technically we're still looking good," said a trader.
